name: Review transitive package chains in candidate and portfolio repositories

attribution.legal_posture: Original researcher-described static package-chain analysis. The reported package behavior and cluster attribution are source claims rather than an adjudication; package names and live selectors are omitted pending independent status and technical verification.

caveats: Package blocking or attribution requires evidence beyond name similarity, maintainer identity, hosting provider, or one suspicious code pattern.

Name similarity, profile images, avatars, code style, language, geography, account age, follower graphs, stars, forks, contribution volume and repository topic require corroboration before supporting legal identity, nationality, common operator or DPRK affiliation.

Keep applicant messages, resumes, emails, phone numbers, identity documents, biometrics, private repositories, credentials, tokens, payment data, wallets, raw device or network selectors, active infrastructure and copied malware code out of the record.
Accounts described by these sources remain unpublished, uncontacted, unfollowed, unstarred, unforked, unmessaged, and unprobed.
Fake-interview malware remains analytically separate from fraudulent employment unless an exact source explicitly establishes overlap.
Keep DPRK-linked fake-interview malware analytically separate from fraudulent employment unless an exact source establishes overlap.
Source review examined the record; package download, installation, execution, and endpoint contact fall outside the review.
The record scope excludes person, persona, account, organization, repository, domain, contact value, executable code, active infrastructure selector, and applicant artifact.
Researcher-attributed dependency observations remain corroborative review context; unique attribution requires additional evidence.
Researcher-attributed graph or dependency observations remain corroborative and review-only; they function as contextual signals rather than unique attribution.
This normalization omits the three source-published npm package names; their inactive or historical status remains unestablished, and publication is unnecessary for the defensive control.

Treat package names as historical source-reported indicators pending current registry-status and independent technical verification. Keep omitted accounts, domains, contact values, and executable snippets unpublished, and keep this supply-chain finding distinct from employment fraud unless the source explicitly connects them.

Treat researcher and vendor attributions as claims with source, date, confidence, and limitation. Persona and account labels carry source-level identity status; civil identity is outside those labels.
Use multiple independently explainable signals, trained human review, documented reasons, proportional collection, bounded retention, and a correction or appeal path.
Verify exact package status and technical behavior independently before operational blocking; package-name similarity can create false positives.

infrastructure.statement: The source reports a staged npm dependency chain in a repository it attributed to a developer-persona cluster, culminating in remote-code retrieval and dynamic execution. Exact package names are intentionally omitted pending independent status and technical verification.
defensive_use: Resolve and inspect the full transitive dependency graph for candidate, portfolio, interview, and trial repositories before execution.
Flag newly published or low-history packages that imitate common utility names, form tightly timed wrapper chains, or conceal network retrieval and dynamic execution behind debugging language.
Use lockfiles, allowlists, isolated package caches, restricted egress, and independent review before any dependency installation.
Do not infer DPRK attribution from a package name, maintainer account, hosting provider, or one suspicious code pattern alone.
